The word may come from the Arabic word for drum, but the earliest evidence shows it developing out of instruments native to South Asia; Vedic-period texts already mention drum structures. The reliefs of the Bhaja caves of the second century BC, the Ajanta cave paintings from before the fifth century BC and some temple carvings all show small paired drums or pushkara drums, which shows that they were widespread in ancient India. There are clear images from about 1745, the form kept developing into the early 1800s, and from the eighteenth century it became the main percussion instrument of North Indian classical music.

A black disc called the syahi is pasted at the centre of the head, made from a tuning paste of iron filings, flour and glue. The head is held by a leather strap passed through small holes in the body and wound sixteen times, with small wooden pegs (gatta) wedged between the straps, and the tension is adjusted with the lacing. The body of the instrument may be wood, clay or metal; the source does not describe specific metal or clay versions of the treble drum.

The dayan, the treble drum of the tabla, belongs to the membranophone hand drums of South Asia, Hornbostel–Sachs number 211.11. It is used in pairs with the bass drum; the body is usually hollowed from a hardwood such as rosewood or mango wood, about fifteen centimetres across, the head is goatskin, and the tension is set with leather straps and wooden pegs. The player strikes the centre and the rim of the head with palm and fingers, and different strokes give different pitches; in North Indian classical music these strokes are built into rhythmic patterns and improvised on, and the drum can also play solo, accompany or join an ensemble. It is found in the traditional, popular and folk music of India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, as well as in Sufi music, devotional singing and kathak dance.
塔布拉鼓音色兼具明亮與溫潤的特質，具有豐富的層次感。高音鼓達顏音色清脆明亮，具有: The tabla's timbre is both bright and warm, with many layers. The treble dayan is crisp and bright and carries strongly, while the bass bayan is deep and dark with a long resonance. Different striking positions and techniques give a range of sounds, from a clear slap to a low, muffled tone. The range is wide, spanning several octaves from a low rumble to a bright ring. Its way of resonating is unusual: pressing the head with the fingers changes its tension, so the pitch and the tone can be adjusted as you play, which makes the sound flexible and expressive. Compared with the heaviness of the Western timpani, the tabla is finer and more nimble; compared with African drums, it carries more of the elegant flavour of Indian classical music, clearly layered and strongly rhythmic.
演奏塔布拉鼓時，右手擊較小的達顏（高音鼓），左手擊較大的巴顏（低音鼓）。發聲以手: When playing the tabla, the right hand strikes the smaller dayan (treble drum) and the left hand the larger bayan (bass drum). The sound is made by striking the centre and rim of the head with the palm or fingers, and different strokes give different pitches; pressing the heel of the left palm on the head and sliding it forward changes the pressure on the drumhead and with it the pitch. The order to learn is: first the various strokes and the pitches they give, then the rhythmic patterns (theka) built from the strokes (bol), and then improvisation over the continuously repeating avartan cycle. Tuning is done with the leather straps, the wooden pegs and a small hammer tapped on the rim, which sets the tension of the head.
